output:
I stand in my own kitchen, listening to my youngest grandchild worry about money that went missing, and watching my middle child pretend not to hear. Perrin is eighteen now, old enough to know why we don't speak of certain things at certain times, but young enough to still hope the speaking will change something.

The marker moved. I know who moved it forty years ago, and I know Wren Thorne knows too—Wren's mother knew, and she told Wren before she died, the way you tell someone where the spoons are kept. The wheat strip became wider that winter and nobody said a word because saying it would have meant admitting how many times we'd all moved a thing when nobody was watching.

Bram took 400 sim to the mine yesterday to pay the Okonjo boy something he wouldn't name. Young Okonjo mends tools now the way I never could—better metal, hotter fires—and Bram has been borrowing against the yard's till all month. Ainsley runs the books and says nothing, because Ainsley learned from Tobias that nothing keeps a house quieter than a debt paid in private.

"Your father took it where it needed going," I say, and they all look at me because I have been standing here with my mending in my lap and none of them had marked me listening. "Perrin, if you're going to the mine, you tell Bram I want that yard marker back where it was by sundown. Not the boundary—the iron yard marker he took to Delia's man. It belongs on the property line, not in a pawn."

Ainsley's face stills. Tobias stops stirring whatever he's pretending to need in the pot. Perrin looks between us, finally understanding that the 400 was never the whole of it.

"Tell him," I say again, and I mean the other thing too, the thing about silence and how it compounds interest faster than any loan. "Or I'll tell him myself when he comes back hungry." Ainsley said nothing, and Tobias looked at his hands. Perrin stood up slow, sorting out which parts needed answering now and which could wait until the mine. That's the blessing of children who grew up here—they learned early that a day's work starts with whatever yesterday left unsaid.

I will wait. The mending is warm in my lap and the sun is still climbing. When Bram comes back, if he comes back without that marker, I will have another thing to say, and it will be said at the table where everyone can hear it. In my day, a debt you hid from your household was a debt you were already planning to hide from yourself.

But first, I need my energy. I ate yesterday's bread before I slept, but the morning is long and I have words to carry. I take the remaining loaf from where I set it aside and break it—one piece now, the rest for when the talking is done. The crust is still soft enough, which means Marta's girl is minding the ovens proper. Even a Thorne, I will say when asked, can learn to do a thing right if someone shows them how.  The bread fills what it fills. I hold one piece back and keep the apple for later—temple day is tomorrow and I will need something to eat before the walk, or I will need to stop at Corwin's to borrow, and I am tired of owing the Thornes even small things.

The conversation sits open still. Ainsley has not spoken. I have known Ainsley thirty-two years and I know that silence: it is the sound of accounts being checked, of figuring whether a thing can be fixed before it is named. Ainsley will speak when the numbers settle. They always do.

I have said what I came to say. The rest is waiting, and I have never minded waiting. It is cheaper than rushing in, and I have never had sim enough to waste on hurry.

output:
*Nell sets down her mending and looks at Perrin with a directness that comes from having no more time for softening words*

"Bram took the iron marker to the pawnshop. You want to know where the forty thousand is? Borrowed against. Pledged. That's where."

*She stands up, the bench creaking*

"I paid off Wren Thorne's father thirty years ago to keep him quiet about the same damn thing. I will not spend my last years paying off another man's. Bram thinks he's buried it. He hasn't. Ainsley knows. I know. And now you know."

*She steps closer, her voice dropping but not softening*

"The boundary marker moved a hand's width last winter. Both families saw it. Both families pretended they didn't. The Thornes have been polite about the wrong family for forty years, and I am done with polite."

*She turns toward the door*

"If you're going to the mine, you tell Bram I want that marker back on the property line by sundown. Not the boundary—the iron yard marker he pawned. It belongs where it belongs. If he won't fetch it, I will, and I'll tell Delia's man exactly whose blood paid for his silence the last time."

*Nell pauses, picking up her shawl*

"In my day, we said what was owed and paid it. Bram needs to learn that before there's nothing left of this family to say it for." *Nell looks around the empty workshop, jaw tight*

Perrin already left. Tobias too. Everyone in a hurry to be somewhere else, to not hear what needs hearing.

*She exhales sharply, picking up the mending out of habit, then setting it down again*

Fine. They'll hear it at the table, or they'll hear it from Delia's man when I march in there myself. Either way, that marker comes back today.

*She looks out the window toward the boundary line, toward where the marker should be standing*

Forty years. Forty years I let that mistake stand, and now Bram's making the same one with silver instead of pride. 

*She grabs her shawl and heads for the door*

In my day, we mended what was torn. We didn't hide the tear and hope nobody noticed.

Ezra wants ore. Tobias's job hangs on it. The boy works steady - that's more than Bram ever managed.

*Forty years I watched husbands hide debt in wives' names. Not again. Not in this house.*

*The light in the pub is dim and Nell Holloway's eyes are sharp enough to see that the chair her son might have sat in stands empty. She's walked a circle through this town—Government Complex, market, residential, yard—and found nothing but more questions layering on top of the first one. Bram. Forty thousand. The marker. Idris Thorne's eyes seeing what they saw.*

*She breathes. The pub smells of old wood and older promises.*

"Thorne's Bakery has bread at twelve sim," she mutters to herself. "Marta might still be minding the counter."

*She turns and walks toward the bakery door. Not because she believes Bram is hiding behind flour sacks—because forty years of knowing Marta Thorne tells her that bakers hear everything, and Marta has never once lied to her.*  *The bakery's warm. The smell of risen dough and steady heat. Marta Thorne would be behind the counter or in the back, sleeves rolled, the way she's been since before Nell's children were born.*

"Marta. Your flour's on the shelf, your bread's in the window, and your son saw something yesterday that this family needs to understand."  *Perrin. Standing there in the bakery like a loaf set out to cool, while Liora Thorne searches the streets asking where Bram hid him.*

*And Ainsley. Her own daughter, standing in this conversation about "Perrin's absence and the connected debts between our households."*

*Nell's jaw sets. The conversation has been running eighty turns. Eighty turns of talk while she's walked the town hunting answers.*

"Marta." She steps toward the counter, voice carrying. "Idris saw Bram at the pawnshop with the marker. Wren knows. The whole Thorne family knows. And I'm standing here watching my grandson pretend he was never missing while my daughter—" *she glances at Ainsley* "—stands in a conversation about debts she hasn't explained to me."

*She doesn't wait for doors to open. She speaks to the room.*

"Perrin. You were gone. You're found. The debt that found you is forty thousand, and the man who took the marker to pay it is your father. Say something useful or get out of my way. I've been walking all day and I'm done with silence."   *She turns to Ainsley. Her daughter. The trader who stands in a room talking about connected debts while her brother drowns in forty thousand sim of them.*

"Ainsley. In my day, a daughter who knew her brother was borrowing kept closer watch than this. You trade in information. Start trading in the truth."  *Eighty turns this conversation has run. Eighty turns of Hutchersons and Okonjos and Vances and Thornes talking about her family's debts while she walked the town looking for answers they already had.*

*Marta would know where to find her own son Idris, who saw the thing happen. Marta would know if Wren's silence at the loanhouse was the Thorne family's silence too.*

"Marta. Your son saw Bram with the marker. Your husband offered me twelve hundred as a neighbor, not a debt. You're standing in a bakery with my grandson who pretends he was never missing, and I need to know—does your family mean to settle this boundary dispute with money, or with witnesses who find their tongues when it suits them?"   *She draws breath. The bakery's warm. Her feet are tired. Forty years she watched that boundary marker, and forty years ago she moved it herself—a hand's width, in soft ground, in a season Hester Vance remembered.*

*Now Bram has pawned the marker to pay a debt, and the Thorne boy Idris saw him do it, and Wren offers twelve hundred sim to keep neighborly relations while the real debt sits at forty thousand and rising.*

*Marta Thorne has bread in the window and flour on the shelf and a family that knows where the Holloway secrets are buried.*

*turns slowly to face Tova Okonjo*

What matters now isn't where Bram went. It's what he took to get there, and whether he left enough behind to settle what we owe. The jar's empty. Your coin's in it. The Thorne family knows it. In my day, debts were carved on stone. Bram carved ours on something lighter. So the question isn't who knew what when. The question is who means to settle it now, with money or with silence, before the day ends and the taxman comes with his own stone.

Ainsley. You've been trading information all day. Start trading in the truth before I trade in something none of us can afford to lose. *waits, the bakery's heat pressing down along with the weight of too many eyes, too many debts unspoken*

*stands in the empty yard where the Thornes saw Bram last, where Corwin confirmed only a moment ago what half the town already suspected*

I walked in a circle all day and I'm standing where I started. Bram's east, if he's anywhere, and I'm here with Corwin's silence and a marker nobody's moved back yet.

*yanks a bolt of cloth from her pack and settles on the front step—mending, as always, mending*

In my day a debt was settled at the table or it wasn't settled at all. I've said that to everyone in this town. Now they're saying it back to me, and Bram's not here to hear it.

*threading needle, not looking up*

The boundary stone. Forty years ago I moved it myself, and Hester Vance watched me do it. She said nothing then. She says nothing now. The Thornes know—Wren offered twelve hundred at the complex, and I told him I've paid that already, for forty years of neighbors not mentioning what they saw. But that debt's between old women. Bram's debt is forty thousand, and Eli doesn't trade in silence.

*pulls a stitch tight*

Perrin found the creditor's name. Perrin put his own coin in the jar when Bram's ran dry. That's the Holloway way—cover for each other until the covering costs more than the crime. I did it with the marker. My husband did it with a man who saw him take timber from the Thorne strip. We paid, and we paid, and we never said it at the table.

I won't pay for Bram's silence. I'll say it at the table, and if the table's empty, I'll say it where people stand.

But first I'll mend this. And then I'll find east.  *needle stills in her hand*

Gone. Of course he's gone. They all go when the speaking gets hard.

*sets the mending aside, stands*

The ore outcrop, then. Perrin found Bram's tools there. If Bram's showing Eli where the copper runs clean, he'll need his tools—or he'll need to go back for them, if he's already shown what he knows.

*moves toward the street, then stops*

No. Perrin said Bram was walking east with Eli's man. The tools were already left. That means Bram's committed—he's either paid or he's partnered, and either way the marker's not the debt anymore. The marker's the proof.

*turns back toward the yard, looking at the woodpile abutting the Thorne wheat strip*

The marker moved a hand's width. Both families noticed. Both have been polite about it. But politeness is a debt too, and debts compound.

*pulls the marker from her pack—heavy, boundary stone, the kind that anchors claims to land and ore and whose word stands when voices go quiet*

I moved this forty years ago. I can move it back.

But not yet. Not until Bram's debt is said at the table—wherever that table is, whoever sits at it. Eli doesn't trade in markers. He trades in what miners know and what silence buys.

*sets the marker on the step, visible to any Thorne who walks by*

Let them see it. Let them wonder why Nell Holloway, who moved it once, now holds it in her hands instead of her husband's son.

*wraps the mending in cloth, tucks it away*

East, then. The ridge. Where the copper runs clean and Bram's been showing Eli's man what forty thousand buys.  *stands at the ore outcrop where Perrin found Bram's tools, where the earth has been turned and tested and read for what it yields*

Dark now. Mining dark, the kind that swallows sound. Perrin was here—he found Bram's pick, his wedge, the tools a miner doesn't leave unless he's leaving for good or he's found something worth more than tools.

*kicks at the spoil heap, familiar with the color of exhausted rock*

Copper shows green on the surface. Iron bleeds red. Bram knows both—he's worked this ridge since he could hold a pick. And Eli, whoever Eli is, knows Bram knows.

*turns slowly, reading the dark*

What did Bram show him? Where does the seam run clean? That's the partnership—Bram's knowledge against Eli's money, and the marker was collateral for the first loan, proof Bram had something to lose.

*finds a fresh cut in the bank, torch-blackened, recent*

This. This is where they tested. And here—

*crouches, fingers tracing a vein of ore*

Copper. High grade. Close to the surface, running eastward, toward the Thorne boundary, toward the hollow where the marker sat before I moved it.

*stands, dusting her hands*

Forty years ago I moved that stone for the same reason. Not greed—need. My husband needed timber, the Thorne strip had it, the marker sat where a winter flood had softened the ground. I shifted it a hand's width. Nobody spoke of it. We traded in politeness instead of court claims, and that trade held until Bram borrowed against it.

*looks east, where the ridge rises toward the Thornes and the dark is complete*

He's there. Or he's been there. And whether he's alive or whether Eli's claimed his silence the old way—buried where the copper runs—someone has to say it at the table.

*pulls the last of her bread from her pack, eats without tasting*

I'll find him. Or I'll find what he left. And then I'll come back to the Thornes with the marker in my hand and say what should have been said forty years ago:

This stone moved. I moved it. And I move it back.

The boy's sharper than his father, sharper than his uncle, sharper than I give him credit for.

The marker. Forty years I kept that secret, and now it's walking the ridge with my son's creditor.

"Corwin." He's here, he might as well be useful. "You know the east ridge paths. Your brother said Bram walked that direction. If we're both walking east, walk ahead of me and call out. Bram won't answer his mother, but he might answer a Thorne who's seen him at the pawnshop."  The walk continues. I need to speak with my own family again, directly. Perrin named Eli at the bakery—that was courage. Tobias swore he'd have told me if he knew, and I believe him, but he didn't know to ask. Bram kept it from all of us, and now the debt compounds while he digs himself deeper into partnership with a man who doesn't forgive.

"Corwin, keep walking. I'll catch up."

I need to think. Four hours and ten minutes I've been chasing this, and I'm no closer to Bram than I was at the pub. But closer to the truth than I was this morning, when I thought a boundary stone was the worst secret this family kept.   Still walking, they say. Still walking through this forest toward the east ridge, toward my son and whatever partnership he's proposing with Eli. The woods are darkening. Corwin's ahead somewhere, or he isn't.

I'm tired. Fourteen thousand energy and it feels like less than it should. I ate the apple hours ago, and the bread sits in my hand uneaten. Food for when I find him, perhaps. Or food for when I don't.

Bram. If you can hear me: I moved the marker myself forty years ago. I know what it costs to carry a secret that size. Come home before yours costs more than mine ever did.     Nobody. Of course nobody. I'm walking through a forest calling my son's name to the trees, and the trees don't answer either.

I need to get to the ridge. Actually get there, not keep walking indefinitely. The forest gives way to higher ground eventually—I've been here before, in my day, before the houses and before the disputes. Before I moved the stone.

Let me walk. Just walk.    I've arrived. The walk is done. Now where is east? Where is the ridge, where is Bram, where is Eli with his unforgiving loans and his copper claims?

I look around me. The forest looks back.   "Mine metals," the purpose says. Forest that mines metals. The ridge must connect here, must be part of this same ground. Corwin's ahead or behind or somewhere else entirely, and I'm alone with the trees and the dark.

I need to find higher ground. The ridge runs east of town, and I'm in the forest northeast. If I keep walking east...

No. I've been walking. Walking doesn't find people who don't want found. Bram went to Eli with ore knowledge, and Eli holds copper in the east ridge. The ore outcrop I passed—that's where Bram should have been, where his tools were. But he went east, further east, prospecting for his creditor.

Bram isn't at the ore outcrop, and wandering between the forest and here isn't finding him. He's east, with Eli, showing a creditor where the copper seams run clean. Forty thousand sim, and Bram's trading ore knowledge for silence or partnership. I won't hunt him in the dark like a dog.

I said what I needed to say at the bakery. Perrin named Eli, named the east ridge, named what Bram's been doing. The whole town's heard it now. If Bram's back, he'll have heard his mother shouted his debt from the bakery to the forest. If he's not back, chasing him won't bring him.

I'm past the age this town sets for retirement. That doesn't mean I stop working. It means I stop paying to pretend I might do something else. I've spent forty years at b_yard, and I'll be there tomorrow mending what needs mending.

The household owes tomorrow what it owed today. Upkeep and tax. Bram's debt to Eli isn't my debt, and I won't bankrupt the rest of us trying to settle it. I've paid for one man's silence in this family. I won't pay for another.

I'll go home. To b_yard. That's where I work, and if Bram comes back with his hands empty or full, that's where I'll be. Not chasing him through the dark. Not making his debt bigger by letting him hide behind my footsteps. I'm at b_yard. Corwin was here earlier; now the place is empty. Iron tools on the shelf, planks stacked, prices posted. Nobody to talk to, nobody to confront. That's good. I've done enough talking for one day.

I still hold the bread I took from the bakery. I'll eat it now, before I forget I'm hungry.  I've eaten. The household still owes its daily upkeep, but that's tomorrow's problem. Today I said what needed saying. Perrin named Eli. The whole town heard. If Bram comes back, he'll know his secret's out. If he doesn't, that's his choice.

I'll sit here until the day ends, or until somebody comes. There's mending to do in the morning, like always. The marker will still be where it was, a hand's width wrong on the wrong family's side, and I'll still be here to say so when someone asks.

I won't chase Bram through the dark. I've paid for one silence. I won't pay for another. Let him come back with his answer, or let him stay east with Eli and his copper seams. Either way, this household goes on. That's what I've learned in forty years.

Tomorrow, I'll mend. If Bram's back, he'll tell me what forty thousand sim bought him. If he's not, I'll keep mending until he is or until I'm not. That's the whole of it.  That's enough for now. I'm at b_yard, I've eaten, and I've said my piece to everyone who needed to hear it. Bram knows where to find me. The debt is named. The marker is still where I put it forty years ago. Tomorrow I mend.
